families.outcome: Read a short descriptive/reportage passage and move from retrieval to inference to judging the writer's attitude
families.context: Original 112-word passage: a night baker in Rose Hill, reprinted in full in every variant

variants.variation: retrieve a number stated in words and write it in figures
variants.misconception: copies a nearby number (half past ten) without checking what it counts

variants.variation: infer something the passage never states (his isolation) from combined details
variants.misconception: picks the most vivid image (the smell of flour) as though vividness were evidence

variants.variation: produce the word carrying a given meaning rather than choose it
variants.misconception: answers 'complain', the neighbouring and more familiar verb

variants.variation: weigh the strength of the writer's attitude, not just its direction
variants.misconception: reads any criticism as contempt

variants.variation: select the quotation that supports one exact claim among four accurate quotations
variants.misconception: picks a quotation that mentions the topic instead of one that supports the claim

families.outcome: Follow an argument through a short opinion column and judge a claim about the writer's position
families.context: Original 120-word school-magazine column on phones in lessons

variants.variation: retrieve a duration in the writer's own words
variants.misconception: supplies a plausible length (a year) instead of the printed one

variants.variation: explain the effect of a structural device (matched sentence shapes)
variants.misconception: assumes the side named first is the side the writer supports

variants.variation: identify the distinction the argument turns on (owning vs using)
variants.misconception: takes a mid-argument detail (the toilets) as the writer's point

variants.variation: quote evidence accurately, with the sequence of events checked
variants.misconception: quotes 'the box', which is the later solution, not where phones went during the ban

variants.variation: judge a pupil's claim against the whole column; all four options are developed
variants.misconception: lifts a concession out of an argument and treats it as the conclusion

families.outcome: Compare two texts on one event: shared facts, added detail, apparent contradiction, difference of purpose
families.context: TWO original texts on the same footpath repair — a council notice (65 words) and a resident's letter (90 words), both reprinted in every variant

variants.variation: find the one fact carried by both texts
variants.misconception: a detail remembered clearly from one text is assumed to be in both

variants.variation: add what the second text says about a fact the first reports flatly
variants.misconception: assumes everything a complaining text mentions is unfinished

variants.variation: resolve an apparent contradiction: disagreement about sufficiency is not a clash of facts
variants.misconception: treats any difference of tone, or a comparison of two different jobs, as a contradiction

variants.variation: contrast the purposes of the two texts
variants.misconception: reads 'thanks residents for their patience' as an apology

variants.variation: name the text type from its opening and its voice
variants.misconception: answers 'notice' or 'report', which describe the other text

families.outcome: Read a non-continuous text (headed leaflet with a list) for information and for how it is organised
families.context: Original school-library Reading Week leaflet with three headings, four listed events and a capacity figure

variants.variation: retrieve from a list where two entries share a time
variants.misconception: searches for the time and stops at the first match

variants.variation: explain why a list is used rather than prose
variants.misconception: assumes layout signals importance rather than how the text will be used

variants.variation: place a NEW sentence under the right heading — organisation, not retrieval
variants.misconception: matches a repeated word ('pupils') to a heading instead of matching purpose

variants.variation: infer why a capacity figure was printed beside a sign-up instruction
variants.misconception: brings in knowledge of other halls that the leaflet does not supply

variants.variation: judge a claim about the leaflet's audience by auditing all four events
variants.misconception: judges audience from the title ('Reading Week') rather than from what the text asks readers to do

families.outcome: Read a narrative extract for its devices, its implications and the words that evidence them
families.context: Original 75-word extract: a teacher, an emptied classroom and one bag left behind

variants.variation: name the device rather than select it from a list
variants.misconception: answers 'metaphor' having seen a comparison but not the signal word 'like'

variants.variation: read a figurative statement about size correctly; all distractors are literal readings
variants.misconception: takes 'gone suddenly enormous' as a physical measurement

variants.variation: infer a habit from a time reference, against a tempting causal detail
variants.misconception: uses the opening detail (a nine-second exit) as the cause of the closing one

variants.variation: supply a word used outside its usual field (a liquid verb used of noise)
variants.misconception: answers 'finding' because it sits inside the same water image

variants.variation: produce the exact two words that evidence 'for a long time'
variants.misconception: quotes 'She knew', which evidences knowing but not duration

families.outcome: Read a table plus its footnote: retrieve, explain the layout, apply a constraint, and identify missing information
families.context: Original Curepipe-to-Rose Hill bus table (4 services, 3 timing points) with a note on the days of operation. Journey times are internally consistent: route 198 = 40 min, route 22 = 46 min on both runs

variants.variation: read across a row to the correct column
variants.misconception: reads the intermediate (Phoenix) column instead of the destination

variants.variation: explain why a footnote sits outside the table
variants.misconception: treats position on the page as a ranking of importance, and skips the note

variants.variation: apply a deadline constraint: LATEST departure that still arrives in time
variants.misconception: reads 'latest' from the departure column and ignores the arrival condition

variants.variation: identify what the text does NOT tell you before answering a question with it
variants.misconception: treats a stated exception ('not on public holidays') as a complete list of the days covered

families.outcome: Follow where a passage of complaints actually arrives, and evidence it
families.context: Original 100-word passage: an unplanned mango tree behind the science block

variants.variation: retrieve a number from among three competing numbers
variants.misconception: takes '7' from 'the Grade 7s' or '2' from 'two slabs'

variants.variation: supply the verb carrying a given meaning
variants.misconception: answers 'drops', the neighbouring verb in the same list

variants.variation: infer WHY an annual suggestion always dies, from the timing the passage gives
variants.misconception: reverses the text — thinks the beans benefit from the shade

variants.variation: match evidence to a claim about origin rather than about nuisance
variants.misconception: offers evidence about the general subject instead of the exact claim

variants.variation: judge a claim about the writer's position against the shape of the whole passage
variants.misconception: counts negative details instead of following where the argument lands; reads a concession as the view

families.outcome: Produce the conventions of a formal letter and control its register
families.context: A pupil's formal letter to the head teacher about a broken water fountain

variants.variation: produce the salutation for an unnamed reader
variants.misconception: writes 'Dear Head Teacher' (a job title where English uses a name) or 'Hello Sir'

variants.variation: produce the closing that the given salutation forces
variants.misconception: reverses the faithfully/sincerely pair

variants.variation: ONE condition changed — the reader is now named; the same question has a different answer
variants.misconception: believes the closing depends on formality or on the subject, not on the salutation

variants.variation: locate the single word that breaks the register in a sentence that is otherwise fine
variants.misconception: rewrites the whole sentence, or blames a neutral noun

variants.variation: choose among four requests that differ only in register
variants.misconception: confuses formal with forceful ('It is about time'), or thinks 'please' alone makes a sentence formal

families.outcome: Diagnose and repair cohesion faults in a pupil's own paragraph
families.context: A five-sentence numbered paragraph about a bottle collection, with one gap and one ambiguous pronoun

variants.variation: supply a connective after naming the relationship
variants.misconception: chooses 'However' because the paragraph contains a surprise — a surprise is not a contrast

variants.variation: diagnose someone else's wrong answer and say why it is wrong
variants.misconception: invents a placement rule ('however cannot begin a sentence') instead of naming the meaning fault

variants.variation: locate an ambiguous pronoun rather than being told where it is
variants.misconception: checks what the writer meant instead of what the nearest preceding noun is

variants.variation: produce the repair, not the diagnosis (first two words only, so marking stays closed)
variants.misconception: avoids repeating a noun because repetition was taught as a style fault

families.outcome: Plan and judge argumentative writing: relevance, reason vs example, topic sentences, evidence that fits its claim
families.context: The essay title 'Should the school day start an hour later?' with a pupil's four-point plan, a drafted body paragraph, and a second pupil's rival plan

variants.variation: classify a point by which side it argues for
variants.misconception: confuses point 4 with point 3's weakness (a single outside example)

variants.variation: distinguish an example from a reason and name it by number
variants.misconception: treats a concrete example as an argument because it feels solid

variants.variation: choose the topic sentence that makes the paragraph's claim
variants.misconception: announces the topic ('In this paragraph I am going to…') or opens with a general truth

variants.variation: analyse a whole drafted paragraph and name its most serious weakness
variants.misconception: over-generalisation — six pupils in one class used to prove a claim about the whole school

variants.variation: compare two whole plans and justify which produces the stronger essay
variants.misconception: believes a one-sided plan is more convincing, and that answering an objection is a distraction

families.outcome: Proof-read a draft: apostrophes, capitals, direct speech, and the spellings pupils most often correct wrongly
families.context: Sentences taken from a pupil's draft, each presented with its own context

variants.variation: restore a capital letter mid-sentence
variants.misconception: capitalises only after a full stop, the first rule taught

variants.variation: produce the word with the apostrophe in place, having decided how many owners there are
variants.misconception: writes teacher's for a plural owner

variants.variation: punctuate direct speech: where the question mark goes and what happens to the reporting verb
variants.misconception: capitalises 'asked' because a question mark usually ends a sentence

variants.variation: find and correct the misspelling in a sentence containing a decoy
variants.misconception: 'corrects' grateful to greatful on the assumption that it comes from great

variants.variation: apply the consonant+y to -ily rule in production
variants.misconception: spells what the word sounds like when said quickly (necessarly)

families.outcome: Show rather than tell; keep a viewpoint; cut what does not move a story
families.context: Sentences and openings from pupils' descriptive and narrative drafts

variants.variation: distinguish showing from telling among four sentences with the same content
variants.misconception: believes an intensifier ('extremely nervous') counts as showing

variants.variation: identify the one word that instructs the reader's feeling
variants.misconception: deletes the precise verb ('struggled') instead of the feeling word — the opposite of the lesson

variants.variation: locate the word that breaks first-person viewpoint
variants.misconception: uses 'you' as a neutral 'one', which addresses the reader and drops the narrator

variants.variation: cut the sentence that does not change the narrator's situation
variants.misconception: keeps background facts because they look like research

families.outcome: Convert a group-chat message into a school notice: register, precision and accuracy
families.context: One unpunctuated chat message that must be reissued as a notice on the school board

variants.variation: expand a contraction for formal writing
variants.misconception: leaves contractions in place because they read naturally

variants.variation: replace a spoken shortening with its full form
variants.misconception: judges by whether the reader will understand rather than by where the text is printed

variants.variation: expand an abbreviated day and capitalise it
variants.misconception: corrects only the capital and keeps the abbreviation ('Fri')

variants.variation: choose the opening line; one distractor has near-acceptable register but is factually wrong
variants.misconception: writes 'cancelled' for an event that is being postponed

variants.variation: decide which vagueness actually stops the notice working
variants.misconception: thinks the missing cause matters more than the missing date

families.outcome: Name a device, explain its effect, read a literal line correctly, and support a reading with the right words
families.context: Original six-line poem: the sea taking a sea wall stone by stone. Written to answer the audit's two seeds on this pack (g9eng-litv-077 weak-distractors, g9eng-litv-097 format-gap)

variants.variation: name the device in production
variants.misconception: answers 'personification' — true of the poem, but not of the line asked about

variants.variation: say which qualities a simile actually lends; no distractor is a silly literalism
variants.misconception: imports the whole source situation (money, debt, repayment) instead of the borrowed quality

variants.variation: recognise a LITERAL line inside a figurative poem — the reverse of the usual error
variants.misconception: reads everything as figurative once a poem has used a simile

variants.variation: PRODUCE the supporting quotation instead of recognising a developed answer
variants.misconception: copies the whole line, showing where to look but not which words carry the point

variants.variation: four responses, all developed and all quoting accurately; judge the fit between claim and evidence
variants.misconception: picks the response that sounds most developed, or accepts a correct quotation as proof of the claim attached to it

families.outcome: Transform between voices in production, keep the tense, and explain why a writer chose the passive
families.context: Short news-style sentences about a council, a head teacher and an inspection

variants.variation: produce the passive, agent kept, tense held
variants.misconception: shifts to the present perfect while changing the voice

variants.variation: reverse the transformation — passive back to active
variants.misconception: keeps 'was' out of habit and produces a sentence in neither voice

variants.variation: hold the present perfect through the transformation
variants.misconception: defaults to the simple past because most passive practice sentences are past

variants.variation: explain the writer's REASON for the passive, not the form of it
variants.misconception: believes the passive is a rule of newspapers, or that the active would be ungrammatical

notes: 71 variants across 15 families — slightly above the 50-65 guidance, on the coordinator's instruction to give g9eng-reading a real spread at every level. 62 of the 71 (87%) went to the two starved chapters.

33 of 71 items (46%) are makeText in a pack that was 100% MCQ. Every typed answer is a closed set: one word, a two-word fixed phrase, a sentence number, or a transformation whose opening is dictated by the stem. No item asks for free composition.
Passage stimuli are all original prose written for this bank: 7 passages, a two-text pair, a leaflet, a bus table and a six-line poem. Nothing is reproduced from any source.

DELIBERATE CONTRAST PAIR: g9eng-fam-006-b (Yours faithfully) and -006-c (Yours sincerely) teach the pair by changing one condition. Neither stem discloses the other's answer, but both explanations state the full rule, so they should not be scheduled consecutively. pickSpreadingFamilies() already takes at most one variant per family per exam paper, so this only matters in a deliberate linked-practice sequence.

The bus table was corrected during authoring so journey times are internally consistent (198 = 40 min on both runs, 22 = 46 min on both). Before that fix, g9eng-fam-014-d's distractor 'how long route 22 takes' had two different true answers and would have been unfair.

L4 = 7 items, all extended analysis: judging a claim against a whole argument (002-e, 015-e), resolving an apparent contradiction across two texts (003-c), auditing a whole leaflet against a claim about its audience (004-e), diagnosing a drafted paragraph's over-generalisation (008-d), comparing two whole essay plans (008-e), and choosing between four equally developed, accurately quoted literary responses (011-e). No vocabulary or single-word item is labelled L4.
